title: Lancet Study: Passive Smoking Deaths in India Jump 50% Since 1990
excerpt: Deaths from second-hand smoke in India rose from about 217,700 to 325,600 between 1990 and 2023, with 444 million Indians now exposed — the world's second-highest total after China.
body:
• Deaths attributable to second-hand smoke in India rose from about 217,700 in 1990 to 325,600 in 2023 — an increase of nearly 50%, according to a study in The Lancet Public Health.
  • While the age-standardized exposure rate fell by roughly a third, India's population growth pushed the absolute number of people exposed to second-hand smoke from 375 million to 444 million.
  • India had the world's second-highest number of people exposed to second-hand smoke in 2023, after China.
  • Children account for more than 12% of the world's health burden from second-hand smoke, with lower respiratory infections causing the greatest burden.

Deaths linked to second-hand smoke in India have surged almost 50% since 1990, claiming 325,600 lives in 2023 alone, according to a new study published in The Lancet Public Health on Monday. India had the world's second-highest number of people exposed to second-hand smoke last year, behind China, with 444 million Indians affected.

The paradox at the heart of the findings: while the age-standardized prevalence of exposure in India declined from 43.2% to 30.6% over three decades, population growth more than offset the gains. The absolute number of people exposed rose from 375 million in 1990 to 444 million in 2023 — an increase of 18.4% — and deaths attributable to second-hand smoke climbed from 217,700 to 325,600 during the same period.

Context and Background

The study draws on Global Burden of Disease estimates for 204 countries and territories. Death rates — deaths per hundred thousand population — fell from 46.1 in 1990 to 30 in 2023, down 35%, even as the absolute death toll rose. Fatalities among women rose from 113,400 to 156,900, while deaths among men rose from 104,300 to 168,700. Second-hand smoke also accounted for 9.28 million disability-adjusted life-years, or DALYs, in India in 2023 — healthy years lost to premature death, illness, or disability.

Globally, the study estimated 2.71 billion people were exposed to second-hand smoke in 2023, contributing to around 1.66 million deaths and 44.8 million DALYs. China, India, and Indonesia accounted for nearly half of the world's exposed population, with China recording 664 million exposed people.

Second-hand smoke is linked to ischaemic heart disease, stroke, lung cancer, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, breast cancer, type 2 diabetes, asthma, and lower respiratory infections. Among children, lower respiratory infections were the leading contributor to the disease burden.

Children Bear a Heavy Burden

Children were found to account for more than 12% of the world's health burden from second-hand smoke. "The numbers mean that despite a fall in the adjusted rates, the absolute number of people exposed to passive smoking is still increasing. This can have long-lasting effects across multiple organ systems, not just the respiratory system," Dr. Neetu Jain, pulmonologist and senior consultant at Pushpawati Singhania Hospital and Research Institute in New Delhi, told PTI.

Dr. Jain noted that passive smoking is avoidable if smokers take steps to prevent exposing others — smoking outside the home and away from enclosed spaces can sharply reduce exposure, particularly for children, whose lungs are still developing. "The effects tend to be greatest among those who are least aware of what passive smoking is and the health risks associated with it," she said, urging higher tobacco prices and taxes as part of stronger tobacco-control measures.

"Second-hand smoke contributes not only to illness and disability but also to premature deaths and loss of healthy years. Kids and women are particularly vulnerable, with children's developing lungs making them more susceptible to respiratory issues."

— Dr. G C Khilnani, chairperson of pulmonary and critical care, PSRI Hospital

Impact and Analysis

The findings expose a familiar public-health trap: falling rates that mask a growing crisis in absolute terms. India's tobacco-control efforts — public smoking bans, pack warnings, and the Cigarettes and Other Tobacco Products Act — have cut the share of people exposed, but a growing population means more Indians than ever are breathing someone else's smoke. Women, who often have less power to insist on smoke-free homes, saw deaths rise by more than a third.

The study's authors and the physicians interviewed by Indian media converge on the same prescriptions: smoke-free homes, stronger enforcement of smoke-free public spaces, higher tobacco taxes, and public-awareness campaigns aimed at households where exposure is invisible and unmeasured.

Diaspora Angle

For Indian-American families, the findings land close to home — literally. Many diaspora households include grandparents visiting from India, where smoking indoors remains common, and second-hand exposure in multi-generational homes is easy to overlook. The study's warning about children and women is worth carrying into family conversations, especially when elders visit during the winter months.

What's Next

The Lancet Public Health study adds to a growing body of evidence likely to feature in India's next round of tobacco-control policymaking. Watch for whether the health ministry responds with revised smoke-free rules, steeper taxation, or targeted campaigns on second-hand exposure — and whether state governments move beyond enforcement on paper to action in public spaces.
